content: The control chart, also referred to as the Shewhart chart or process-behavior chart, is a statistical tool used in process control to assess whether a manufacturing or business process is operating within a state of statistical control. If the chart indicates that the process is not in control, the patterns observed can help identify the source of variation, which can then be addressed to restore the process to a controlled state. A control chart is a specific type of run chart and is one of the seven fundamental tools of quality control, alongside the histogram, Pareto chart, check sheet, cause-and-effect diagram, flowchart, and scatter diagram. The control chart was developed by Walter A. Shewhart in the 1920s while working at Bell Labs. The engineers at Bell Labs were focused on improving the reliability of their telephony transmission systems, particularly because the equipment, such as amplifiers, was buried underground, making repairs costly and difficult. By 1920, they recognized the importance of reducing variation in manufacturing processes. They also discovered that frequent process adjustments in response to non-conformance often increased variation and degraded quality. Shewhart conceptualized the problem in terms of common causes and special causes of variation. On May 16, 1924, he introduced the control chart in an internal memo, providing a schematic diagram and a concise explanation of its principles. This memo laid the foundation for modern process quality control. Shewhart emphasized that achieving and maintaining a state of statistical control, where only common-cause variation exists, is essential for predicting future output and managing processes economically. He designed experiments to establish the basis for the control chart and the concept of statistical control. While Shewhart drew from mathematical statistical theories, he understood that data from physical processes do not always conform to a normal distribution (Gaussian distribution or bell curve). He observed that manufacturing data often behaved differently from natural phenomena, such as Brownian motion. Shewhart concluded that while all processes exhibit variation, some display controlled variation inherent to the process, while others show uncontrolled variation caused by external factors. In 1924 or 1925, Shewhart's work caught the attention of W. Edwards Deming, who later became a prominent advocate of Shewhart's methods. Deming worked at the U.S. Department of Agriculture and later as a mathematical advisor to the U.S. Census Bureau. Over the next 50 years, Deming championed Shewhart's ideas, spreading their application widely. After World War II, Deming served as a statistical consultant to the Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers in Japan. His involvement in Japanese industry during the 1950s and 1960s helped popularize Shewhart's control charts in Japanese manufacturing, contributing to their industrial success. More recently, Donald J. Wheeler has continued to promote the use and development of control charts in the Shewhart-Deming tradition. When a process is in control, most data points will fall within the control limits. Observations outside these limits, or systematic patterns within the limits, suggest the presence of a new, unexpected source of variation, known as a special cause. Since increased variation leads to higher costs, the detection of special causes requires immediate investigation. In practice, the long-term process mean (centerline) may not align perfectly with the ideal target value due to equipment limitations or cost constraints. It is generally easier to adjust a process to meet a target than to minimize variability, which reinforces the importance of reducing process variation. Process capability studies examine the relationship between natural process limits (which determine control limits) and specification limits. Warning limits or zones on control charts provide early indications of potential issues. Instead of immediately initiating process improvement efforts, quality engineers may temporarily increase sampling rates to confirm whether the process is truly in control. With three-sigma limits, one expects a false signal approximately once every 370 points due to common causes alone. Shewhart established three-sigma limits based on several considerations: 1. Chebyshev's inequality, which states that for any probability distribution, the likelihood of an outcome exceeding k standard deviations from the mean is at most 1/k². 2. The Vysochanskii-Petunin inequality, which refines this for unimodal distributions, stating that the probability of an outcome exceeding k standard deviations is at most 4/(9k²). 3. Empirical evidence showing that at least 99% of observations fall within three standard deviations of the mean. Shewhart initially experimented with limits based on probability distributions but ultimately emphasized empirical evidence over theoretical justification. He viewed the control chart as a heuristic tool rather than a hypothesis test, rejecting the Neyman-Pearson framework. Deming also argued that the disjoint nature of population and sampling frames in industrial settings undermines conventional statistical techniques. Control charts aim to avoid two types of errors: 1. Mistaking a common-cause variation for a special cause (Type I error). 2. Mistaking a special cause for a common cause (Type II error). The calculation of control limits requires the standard deviation of common-cause variation. Traditional estimators based on sample variance are not used, as they include both commonand special-cause variation. Instead, alternative methods, such as using the relationship between sample range and standard deviation derived by Leonard H.C. Tippett, are preferred to minimize the influence of extreme observations. Rules for detecting signals include the Western Electric rules, Wheeler rules, and Nelson rules. There is debate over how many consecutive points on one side of the centerline constitute a signal, with recommendations ranging from 7 to 9 points. Importantly, rules should be established before analyzing the data to avoid bias. In 1935, the British Standards Institution adopted control charts with limits based on percentiles of the normal distribution, diverging from Shewhart's three-sigma limits. This approach, influenced by Egon Pearson, has been criticized by proponents of the Shewhart-Deming tradition. Control charts are effective at detecting large changes in process mean or variance, as their out-of-control average run lengths (ARLs) are relatively short in such cases. However, they are less efficient at detecting smaller changes, such as a 1or 2-sigma shift in the mean. Alternative charts, such as the EWMA (Exponentially Weighted Moving Average) and CUSUM (Cumulative Sum) charts, are better suited for identifying smaller changes by incorporating information from prior observations. Critics of control charts argue that they violate the likelihood principle, though this principle itself is controversial. Supporters counter that it is often impossible to specify a likelihood function for processes not in statistical control, especially when knowledge of the causal system is limited. Additionally, some authors criticize the use of average run lengths (ARLs) for comparing chart performance due to the high variability inherent in geometric distributions.
